newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy cuts key interest rate to 7.5 percent.
newsitem.headline: Italy cuts key interest rate to 7.5 percent.

text.p: The Bank of Italy took financial markets by surprise when it announced a cut in its key discount rate to 7.5 percent from 8.25 on Wednesday in a strong vote of confidence in government efforts to wrestle down inflation.
A statement from the central bank said the cut would take effect on Thursday, when its fixed term advances or Lombard rate would also fall to 9.0 percent from 9.75.

The reduction, following a similar 0.75 point cut on July 23, was welcomed by Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose government has been eager for a fall in borrowing costs to help lower the interest bill on Italy's public debt mountain.
"It's a recognition of the validity of the work carried out by the government and a useful encouragement for the path that we still have to pursue," said Prodi immediately after the announcement.
Silvio Berlusconi, leader of the centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance, said the central bank had acted sooner than expected because it was worried about the state of the economy.
"It appears evident to me that the Bank of Italy has brought forward the timing (of the cut) because it is very worried, as are all of us, over the serious economic recession," he said.
The lira weakened after the central bank's move, easing from around 1,002 lire against the mark to 1,006 lire.

The central bank may even follow up with a further interest rate reduction before the end of the year, economists said. Even after the rate cut, Italy's interest rates remain higher than in any other Group of Seven industrialised country.
"We can't completely rule out a small reduction before the end of the year, but we definitely expect a bigger cut by next summer," said Claudio Tosato an economist with Deutsche Bank.
The Bank of Italy made clear its latest move was linked to signs that inflation is on a downward slope.
"The process of moderation in inflationary expectations is under way, towards levels coherent with the aim of inflation firmly below three percent in 1997," it said.
The cut followed publication of preliminary consumer price data by 10 Italian cities on Monday and Tuesday which pointed to an October inflation rate of 3.0 percent year-on-year.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio had said he would not cut rates until year-on-year inflation was below three percent.
This is why many analysts had not expected a cut in interest rates until next month's preliminary inflation figures were out.
Market commentators expressed surprise over the suddenness of the move but they were not taken aback by the size of the cut.

"It looks like they brought things forward. I expect the Bank of Italy will reward the government if they get the budget through and I think we could see seven percent by the end of the year," said Sally Wilkinson of UBS bank in London.
They had been widely expecting the Bank of Italy to cut rates by 75-100 basis points in about a month's time, provided passage of the government's 1997 austerity budget was on track.
The budget is designed to slash a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's deficit and is due to go before the full lower house of parliament from October 28.

The Bank of Italy has previously exercised extreme caution in its conduct of monetary policy. It raised rates twice in 1995 and waited 14 months and resisted considerable political pressure to act before making July's cut.

Final October inflation figures are due out on November 6. If they confirm analyst forecasts of 3.0 percent consumer price inflation, the level would be the lowest since the June 1969 rate of 2.5 percent.
The inflation rate was 3.4 percent year-on-year in September and 5.8 percent in October last year. Prices peaked last year at six percent in November.
